title: A Wardrobe for the Interior
premise: Lior Sandoval, a night librarian who has spent a decade avoiding their estranged family, hears an unrecorded song—written by their late sister Vera—playing on a late-night radio program, proof that someone in the family has been leaking her private compositions. As the last bus route to the old neighborhood faces permanent rerouting, Lior traces the leak through a chain of found-family figures: the radio host, a retired bus driver, and Vera's old bandmate, each holding a piece of the truth about Vera's death, which the family never brought to court because the man responsible was one of their own. The investigation forces Lior home, where the family must finally hold its own reckoning—a trial of memory rather than law. The book ends with the family choosing testimony over silence: the uncle confesses, the neighborhood's last bus makes a final ceremonial run carrying Vera's song, and Lior, no longer a tenant of their own life, becomes the keeper of the family archive.
about_author: P. M. Dunmore is the pen name of a former municipal archivist who spent eleven years cataloguing the papers of defunct transit authorities before turning to fiction. They write at night, in libraries, and claim to have never once taken the express train.

chapters.title: The Hours That Belong to No One
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. We meet the night library, its insomniac regulars, and Lior's philosophy of invisible tenancy—present everywhere, owning nothing. A routine inventory of a donated record collection plants the first seed: an unlabeled cassette. The beat is quiet melancholy, the comfort of a life with no claims on it.

chapters.title: A Song With No Address
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Driving home, the radio plays a melody Lior knows was written by their sister Vera and never recorded—she sang it once, in the kitchen, in 2009. Lior nearly drives off the road. The beat is vertigo: the past reaching through the present, the first crack in the armor of distance.

chapters.title: The Host Who Plays Ghosts
chapters.summary: Radio host Marisol Vega's POV. Marisol explains her practice of airing 'orphan songs' sent to her by anonymous listeners. She guards her sources but recognizes Lior's voice when they call. The beat is wary alliance—two professionals of the night recognizing each other.

chapters.title: Ten Years of Not Calling
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior inventories what they know of the family: mother Odalys, brother Teo, uncle Renán—the man the family arranged itself around after Vera's death, ruled an accident. Lior has attended exactly two gatherings in a decade. The beat is the cost accounting of estrangement.

chapters.title: Route 47, Last Service
chapters.summary: Bus driver Emilio Cadenas's POV, retired, riding his old route before the city reroutes it forever. He remembers Vera as a fare who sang to herself, and remembers the night of her death—details the official report smoothed over. The beat is a city losing its memory in real time, mirroring the family's.

chapters.title: The Cassette in the Donation Box
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The unlabeled cassette proves to contain Vera's home recordings, donated by someone with library access. Lior checks the donor log and finds a name that stops them: R. Sandoval. Uncle Renán has been the leak all along. The beat is betrayal inverted—grief, not malice.

chapters.title: What Renán Carried
chapters.summary: Renán's POV, first time. He has mailed Vera's songs to the radio for two years, one per month, unable to explain why. We see his guilt: he was driving the car the night Vera died, and the family's silence was his sentence. The beat is the weight of unconfessed things.

chapters.title: The Kitchen Where the Song Was Born
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, flashback braided with present. Memory of Vera teaching Lior the melody, the family's old apartment, the promise to never record it—'some things are only true once.' The beat is tender, establishing exactly what was lost.

chapters.title: Teo's Ledger
chapters.summary: Brother Teo's POV. Teo, the family's pragmatist, has kept a literal ledger of who owed what after Vera's death—money, silences, blame. He intercepts Lior's first call home and warns them off. The beat is defensive loyalty; Teo believes silence was mercy.

chapters.title: The Bandmate's Version
chapters.summary: Vera's old bandmate, Nilsa, in her repair shop. She reveals Vera had written a letter—never sent—intending to go to the police about the night of the crash. Nilsa kept the draft for ten years, waiting for someone to ask. The beat is the arrival of evidence that memory alone can't supply.

chapters.title: The Letter Vera Never Sent
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, reading the draft letter. Vera suspected Renán had been drinking; she couldn't decide between justice and family, and died before deciding. Lior realizes the family's arrangement was a verdict rendered without a trial. The beat is fury and grief braided together.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Depot
chapters.summary: Lior and Renán, at the transit depot where the old buses are being decommissioned. Lior lays out everything. Renán neither denies nor confesses; he only says, 'The family decided.' The beat is rising tension—the question shifts from what happened to who had the right to bury it.

chapters.title: Odalys Opens the Door
chapters.summary: Mother Odalys's POV. She has known for ten years and chose the family over the truth, believing a prosecution would kill Renán and orphan the rest. Lior comes home; she lets them in but not all the way. The beat is the terrible tenderness of complicity.

chapters.title: The Arrangement
chapters.summary: Family scene, rotating close-third among Lior, Teo, Odalys. The full architecture of the family's silence is exposed: the paid settlement, the moved funeral, the agreed story. Teo defends it; Odalys wavers; Renán says nothing. The beat is a family discovering its own constitution was written in fear.

chapters.title: Marisol's Broadcast
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She decides to devote an entire night's program to Vera's songs, naming her, inviting 'anyone who knows how she died to call in.' The city listens. The beat is private grief made public—the family's secret now has witnesses.

chapters.title: Calls From the Old Neighborhood
chapters.summary: Multi-voice chapter: neighbors, the corner store owner, a nurse from that night, calling in fragments of memory. Individually small, together they corroborate Vera's letter. The beat is the emergence of a community's parallel court—justice assembling itself outside the law.

chapters.title: Renán at the Microphone
chapters.summary: Renán's POV. He goes to the station uninvited and, live on air, tells what happened: the drinking, the swerve, the family's decision to call it an accident. The broadcast is the climax's first detonation. The beat is confession as self-destruction and release at once.

chapters.title: The Question the Family Arranged Itself Around
chapters.summary: The family, in Odalys's kitchen, all night. The question surfaces: not whether Renán was guilty, but whether love can survive truth. Odalys finally speaks her verdict—she chooses the truth she buried. The beat is the emotional climax: the family's founding bargain torn up in front of everyone.

chapters.title: What the Law Will Not Do
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. They pursue legal accountability and find the statute long expired, the evidence inadmissible. The law offers nothing. Lior must decide what justice means when the courts are closed. The beat is the theme made explicit: justice outside the law must be built by hand.

chapters.title: The Last Bus to the Old Neighborhood
chapters.summary: The final run of Route 47. Emilio drives; the family rides together for the first time in a decade, along with neighbors who answered Marisol's broadcast. At the corner where Vera died, they stop, and Renán speaks her name aloud to the street. The beat is ceremonial, communal, cathartic.

chapters.title: A Wardrobe for the Interior
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, title chapter. Lior catalogs Vera's songs into the library's permanent collection—no longer orphan works but housed, named, owned. Renán, awaiting whatever consequences remain, begins recording testimony for the family archive. The beat is the turn from mourning to stewardship.

chapters.title: Owner, Not Tenant
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, coda. One year later: Lior hosts a monthly night of orphan songs at the library; Marisol broadcasts it; the family gathers without an arrangement holding them together—only choice. Lior signs the library's donor wall, their own name, in ink. The beat is resolution: visibility, at last, chosen freely.
